intro/hello: Welcome to chapter eight. Chapter seven built the network itself: neurons, activation functions, layers.
intro/gap: But a network on paper is not one that trains. In between sit a few decisions that look like housekeeping, and turn out to decide everything.
intro/data: What to do to the data first.
intro/init: What numbers to start the weights at.
intro/bn: How to keep the signal well scaled through many layers.
intro/reg: How to stop the network from memorizing.
intro/why: Each has a short recipe, and a reason behind it. We will see both.
preprocess/matrix: Start with the data as a matrix X: one row per example, one column per feature, like one pixel value.
preprocess/cloud: With two features, each example is a point, and the data set is a cloud.
preprocess/mean: A feature's mean is its average: add up its column, and divide by the number of examples.
preprocess/mu: One mean per feature marks the center of the cloud: the teal cross, mu.
preprocess/center: Subtracting mu from every row is the always-do step. The cloud slides over to sit around the origin.
preprocess/var: Next, spread. The variance squares each distance from the mean, so negatives count too, and averages the squares.
preprocess/sd: Its square root, the standard deviation sigma, is a typical distance from the mean, in the original units.
preprocess/norm: Dividing each column by its own sigma gives every feature a spread of one.
preprocess/units: That matters when features have different units, like meters and dollars. Pixels share one scale, so for images it is optional.
preprocess/tilt: But the cloud was only slid and stretched along the axes, so its tilt remains: the features still rise and fall together.
pca/together: Real features are rarely independent. Neighbouring pixels are usually similar: when one is bright, so is the other.
pca/cov: The covariance matrix records this. For each pair of features, multiply their centered values, and average over the examples.
pca/diag: On the diagonal, a feature paired with itself, that is just its variance.
pca/off: Off the diagonal, positive means the pair rises together. Here most points are high in both or low in both, so the average is positive.
pca/eig: The covariance has special directions, its eigenvectors. The first points along the cloud's longest spread, the second perpendicular to it.
pca/eig2: Each eigenvalue, in S, says how much the data varies along its direction.
pca/rot: Rotate the data into these directions, and the tilt is gone. The off-diagonal covariance is zero: the features are decorrelated.
pca/reduce: The eigenvectors come sorted by variance. Keep the first k, and each example shrinks from D numbers to k: PCA dimensionality reduction.
pca/white: Whitening then divides each rotated coordinate by its own standard deviation, the square root of its eigenvalue.
pca/round: The cloud becomes round: zero mean, no correlation, equal spread.
pca/eps: The catch: the thinnest directions, mostly noise in real data, get stretched the most. A larger epsilon tempers that.
eigen/real: Now real images: CIFAR-10, shrunk to sixteen by sixteen gray pixels. Each image is a point in two hundred and fifty six dimensions.
eigen/cov: So each eigenvector is two hundred and fifty six numbers, and can be drawn as a picture: an eigen-image.
eigen/blobs: Smooth blobs and gradients: broad brightness patterns carry most of the variance, so the top directions are low frequencies.
eigen/keep: Keep k coordinates per image, and rotate back. With twenty four, about eighty five percent of the variance survives.
eigen/sweep: With fewer, the pictures blur. With more, the detail returns.
eigen/twist: The twist: PCA and whitening are not used with ConvNets.
eigen/recipe: ConvNets just zero-center: subtract the mean image, or one mean per color channel.
eigen/bug: And compute that mean on the training set only, then subtract the same mean from validation and test.
eigen/leak: Compute it before splitting, and the test images leak into training. Your test score stops being honest.
init/question: Every weight needs a starting value. Final weights end up about half positive and half negative, so why not start them all at zero?
init/clones: Because if every weight in a layer is equal, every neuron computes the same output.
init/grads: Each then gets the same gradient, and the same update.
init/forever: They stay clones forever: a hundred neurons acting as one.
init/symmetry: Any constant does this. The problem is the symmetry, not the zero.
init/random: Small random numbers break it: draw each weight from a bell curve around zero, with a small spread, like zero point zero one.
init/differ: Every neuron starts a little different, so each learns something different.
init/danger: But in a deep network, small is a dangerous word. To see why, look at what one neuron does to the spread of its inputs.
variance/neuron: One neuron, before its nonlinearity, multiplies each of its n inputs by a weight, and adds them up. Call the sum s.
variance/ev: The expected value of a random quantity is its long-run average, and its variance is the expected squared distance from it.
variance/f1: Three facts. One: variances of independent quantities add.
variance/f2: Two: multiplying by a number a multiplies the variance by a squared.
variance/f3: Three: for independent quantities centered on zero, the variance of a product is the product of the variances.
variance/derive: Now apply them. The sum has n independent terms, each a weight times an input.
variance/law: So the variance of s is n, times the variance of w, times the variance of x.
variance/shrink: With a hundred inputs and weights of zero point zero one, that factor is a hundredth: the variance shrinks a hundredfold.
variance/fix: To keep it, give w a variance of one over n: draw randn, and divide by the square root of n.
deep/setup: The lecture's experiment: push random data through ten layers of a hundred tan h units, and watch each layer's spread.
deep/small: Weights of zero point zero one: the spread shrinks tenfold per layer.
deep/dead: By layer ten, every activation is about zero. The weight gradients are proportional to them, so they vanish too.
deep/big: Weights of one: the sums are huge, and tan h saturates at minus one and plus one.
deep/flat: Out there tan h is flat, so again no gradient flows.
deep/xavier: Now the variance we derived: one over the fan-in, the number of inputs per unit. This is Xavier initialization.
deep/healthy: The spread holds steady, all the way down.
deep/relu: Switch to ReLU, and Xavier starves the deep layers: ReLU zeroes the negative half, halving the variance it passes on.
deep/he: He and colleagues doubled the variance, to two over the fan-in, and the spread holds again.
deep/glorot: Glorot and Bengio's variant averages fan-in and fan-out, to steady the backward pass too.
deep/bias: Biases simply start at zero. So for ReLU networks: weights times the square root of two over n, and zero biases.
batchnorm/drift: Good initialization only helps at the start. As the weights train, each layer's spread drifts.
batchnorm/idea: Batch normalization, from Ioffe and Szegedy in 2015, simply enforces unit Gaussian inputs at every layer, on every step.
batchnorm/diff: Normalizing is differentiable, so it can be a layer that we backpropagate through like any other.
batchnorm/batch: Here is a mini-batch of sixty four examples, two features each, about to enter a tan h. Below: most of what tan h receives sits in its flat tails.
batchnorm/mean: Step one: subtract each feature's mean over the batch.
batchnorm/var: Step two: divide by each feature's standard deviation over the batch. A tiny epsilon avoids dividing by zero.
batchnorm/alive: Now almost nothing is saturated, so gradients can flow.
batchnorm/tilt: Features are normalized one by one, not decorrelated, so the tilt stays.
batchnorm/gamma: Last, multiply by gamma and add beta: two numbers per feature, learned.
batchnorm/undo: With gamma equal to the batch's spread and beta equal to its mean, the original values come back. Normalized is the default, not a cage.
batchnorm/where: BatchNorm goes after a fully connected or convolutional layer, before the nonlinearity.
batchnorm/test: At test time there may be a single example. So in training, each layer keeps running averages of the means and variances.
batchnorm/converge: Test time normalizes with those instead. They start at zero and one, and settle after many batches.
batchnorm/buys: What it buys: better gradient flow, less sensitivity to initialization, and higher learning rates.
batchnorm/noise: Plus a mild regularizing effect, from the noise of random batch mates.
penalties/overfit: A big network can memorize its training set, noise and all, and then fail on anything new. That is overfitting.
penalties/reg: Regularization discourages it. The first kind adds a weight penalty to the loss, with strength lambda.
penalties/l2: L2 adds up the squared weights, times a half. Doubling a weight quadruples its penalty, so big weights are expensive.
penalties/smooth: The model spreads its reliance over many modest weights, and the wild curve calms down.
penalties/decay: Its gradient is lambda times W: every step shrinks each weight toward zero. Hence its other name, weight decay.
penalties/picture: Here is the geometry with two weights. The red dot is the best fit to the data alone, ringed by contours of the data loss.
penalties/circle: The blue circle holds weights with equal L2 penalty. The answer sits where an ellipse just touches it: both weights shrink, neither reaches zero.
penalties/l1: L1 adds up absolute values instead, charging the same per unit of weight, however big.
penalties/corner: Its shape is a diamond, usually touched at a corner. Raise lambda, and one weight snaps to exactly zero.
penalties/sparse: With sixteen weights and three useful inputs, L1 zeroes the useless ones, while L2 only shrinks them. Elastic net mixes both.
penalties/maxnorm: Max-norm is a hard cap: after each update, a neuron's weight vector longer than c, about three or four, is scaled back. Weights cannot blow up.
penalties/bias: Biases usually go unregularized, and one global L2 strength, tuned on validation data, is the norm.
dropout/what: Dropout, from Srivastava, Hinton and colleagues in 2014, is simple and surprisingly effective.
dropout/how: In training, every forward pass keeps each unit with probability p, and zeroes the rest.
dropout/fresh: A new random set for every example and step. At test time, nothing is dropped.
dropout/coadapt: Why it helps: no unit can count on another. A cat detector cannot lean on its one whiskers unit, gone half the time.
dropout/ensemble: Or: each mask picks a thinned sub-network, and each step trains one.
dropout/count: n units give two to the n sub-networks, sharing weights. The full network at test time acts like their average.
dropout/scale: One subtlety is scale. Kept half the time, a unit sends about half its usual input on, so at test time the next layer would suddenly see twice as much.
dropout/inverted: Inverted dropout divides kept units by p during training: doubled, for p of a half.
dropout/expect: On average a unit sends p times h over p, plus nothing: exactly h, as at test time.
dropout/watch: Track one unit's input over many passes. It jumps around, but its running average settles on the test-time value.
dropout/family: Dropout is one case of a recipe: noise in training, averaged away at test time. Data augmentation and DropConnect are cousins.
dropout/practice: In practice: one global L2 penalty, plus dropout with p around a half.
losses/parts: The other part of the loss, the data loss, averages how well predictions match labels. Which one depends on the question.
losses/one: For one correct class, chapter four's choices apply: softmax, or the multiclass SVM.
losses/sq: Some prefer the squared hinge, which squares each margin.
losses/huge: With huge numbers of classes, like every word in a dictionary, the softmax itself becomes the bottleneck.
losses/tree: Hierarchical softmax puts the classes at the leaves of a tree, with a small left-or-right classifier at each branch.
losses/cost: A class then costs only the length of its path. How well it works depends on the tree.
losses/attr: Sometimes an example has several labels, like a photo with many hashtags. Softmax is wrong there: it makes the classes compete.
losses/sigmoid: Instead, each attribute gets its own sigmoid: an independent probability between zero and one.
losses/logloss: Its loss is minus the log of the probability given to the right answer, yes or no.
losses/grad: Any number can be yes at once, and the gradient is just the probability minus the label.
regression/real: For real-valued outputs, like a height or an angle, the loss measures the distance to the target.
regression/l2l1: L2 adds up squared errors. L1 adds up absolute errors.
regression/grads: Under L2, each point pulls in proportion to its error. Under L1, every point pulls equally: only direction matters.
regression/outlier: Thirteen points near a line, plus an outlier. As it moves away, the L2 fit bends toward it.
regression/l1fit: The L1 fit barely notices: the outlier pulls like any other point.
regression/fragile: So L2 is fragile: a few bad targets swamp the gradients. It also demands exact numbers, where softmax just needs the right class to win.
regression/bins: So first ask: could you bin the output and classify? A star rating often works better as five classes, with a confidence for free.
regression/struct: And for whole structures, like graphs, there is the structured SVM, with special solvers, beyond this course.
outro/pre: Subtract the training mean, and divide by the spread if features differ in scale.
outro/init: Initialize with the square root of two over the fan-in for ReLU, and zero biases.
outro/bn: Batch normalization after each layer, before the nonlinearity.
outro/reg: One L2 penalty tuned on validation data, plus inverted dropout.
outro/loss: And a loss that matches the question.
outro/theme: Keep signals at a healthy scale, and do not let the network memorize.
outro/next: Next, open the interactive chapter: every figure here is there to drag and poke, with its code running beside it.
